catalog_quote: Normally each such utterance is a single intonation unit, with a single tonic (marked ' before the most heavily stressed word), but on occasion it consists of two such units (not separated by pause), as shown by a comma placed after the first. [...] The five vowels i, e, a, o and u are distinguished in stressed syllables, with v used to represent a schwa that appears only in unstressed syllables (following Alpher’s (1991) practice for the nearby Yir-Yoront language). The pronunciation of schwa varies considerably according to context, with final vy and vw sounding much like [i:] and [u:] for most speakers. Contrastive stress accent is generally marked acute (´), but the normally stressed syllable is marked grave (`) where stress has become indistinct (and intonation lowered), typically after the tonic in pronouns and sometimes verbs.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Koko-Bera has a contrastive (phonemic) stress accent: its position is not predictable from the word's shape and has to be marked per word (acute). Black 1980 (p.198) says the same ('Stress is contrastive in Koko-Bera') and explains the origin: Proto-Norman-Pama vowel length continues as stress, so stress sits on the historically long syllable (*nya:ka-la > nákal 'saw', but *panytyi[:]l- > pinytyé- 'be burning'); monosyllables show no stress contrast. Vowel quality is tied to stress: the five full vowels occur in stressed syllables, schwa only in unstressed ones.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Black 2010: the normally stressed syllable can lose distinct stress after the utterance tonic, typically in pronouns and sometimes verbs (marked grave). Black 1980 p.203: monosyllables show no stress contrasts; some bound forms (e.g. pumerír 'father's sister') show shifted stress; Black & Koch 1983 p.163: in singing the normal stress position is kept only insofar as it coincides with the musical beat.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress accent in connected narrative text (Black 2010) and in cited lexical/verb forms (Black 1980); Black 2010 also describes a separate phrase-level 'tonic' per intonation unit. Neither source gives a positional rule or a section on stress; the statements are transcription notes by the fieldworker.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Koko-Bera proper (Black: 'properly Kok-Kapér'), AIATSIS Y85, ISO kkp = gugu1254. Black 2010's narrator Gracie Cecil identified as Kok-Papónk (Koko Babangk, ISO okg; Glottolog's retired koko1273 is equated with kkp), a group immediately south of the Koko-Bera; Black treats her text as Koko-Bera. Black 1980's Koko-Bera data are his phonemicisation of Sommer's unpublished material, gathered before his own 1977-78 fieldwork.

sources.note: p.266 Appendix orthography note: 'Contrastive stress accent is generally marked acute (´), but the normally stressed syllable is marked grave (`) where stress has become indistinct (and intonation lowered), typically after the tonic in pronouns and sometimes verbs.' Five vowels distinguished in stressed syllables, schwa only in unstressed syllables; each utterance is one intonation unit with a single tonic. Author's own Kowanyama fieldwork 1977-78. No positional rule.

sources.note: p.198: 'Stress is contrastive in Koko-Bera and probably also in Kok-Nar and is transcribed acute when attested for a form in either language.' p.203: proto vowel length 'would continue as stress' in Koko-Bera (*nya:ka-la > KB nákal 'saw' vs *panytyi[:]l- > KB pinytyé- 'be burning'); monosyllables 'show no stress contrasts in Koko-Bera and Kok-Nar'. Koko-Bera data = Black's phonemicisation of unpublished Sommer data (p.191).
